passage:
Family diary, written by Meena.

Sunday, 5 pm. Varun sat with my father Shankar on the veranda for almost an hour. I watched from the kitchen door. Instead of arguing about the new tax rules, Varun asked, "Nana, what made you feel so strongly about this?" My father spoke of the years he ran a cooperative shop, when prices jumped and the shelves emptied. Varun did not interrupt once; he only nodded and asked one more question.

At the end, Varun said calmly, "I see why it worries you. I think differently about one part, and here's why." My father raised an eyebrow, then laughed and said, "Well, at least you listened." I brought them tea and did not say a word.

qa.q: Where did Varun and Shankar talk?
qa.a: On the veranda, for almost an hour.

qa.q: What does Shankar's laugh at the end suggest he felt?
qa.a: Shankar likely felt heard and a little disarmed, as Varun's calm way of asking softened any defensiveness.

qa.q: What could Varun try in a later conversation to keep the talk open, and why?
qa.a: Varun could keep asking about Shankar's experiences and share a second view in the same calm tone, because curiosity keeps the door open even when opinions differ.

qa.q: How might Meena feel watching from the kitchen door?
qa.a: Meena may feel relieved and quietly proud, since the talk that might have been feared turned warm and was left uninterrupted.

grounding: The student asks the grandfather what shaped his view, listens without interrupting, then calmly shares one personal view.

passage:
Sunday, 14 January. Jeevan's diary.
Ajja and I talked about politics for an hour today, and nobody left the room angry. Writing it down because that has never happened before.
Deepak usually starts it by arguing, so today I tried something different. When Ajja began on how the old party 'built this country', I asked, 'Ajja, what was it like when you were my age? What made you feel that way?'
He talked about 1971, about his father losing the farm, about the first time electricity came to their village and who brought it. I didn't interrupt once. Deepak kept opening his mouth; I kicked him under the table.
At the end, Ajja asked what I thought. I said one thing, calmly: that I care most about jobs for people my age, and I'm not sure any party is doing enough. He nodded. 'Fair,' he said. 'Your worry is different from mine.'
We don't agree. But he said I could come and ask for more stories next Sunday.

qa.q: What does Jeevan care about most, according to the diary?
How did Ajja seem to feel when Jeevan asked about his youth?
qa.a: He seemed glad to be asked and open, sharing memories instead of defending his view.

qa.q: What made the conversation go better than usual?
qa.a: Asking open questions and listening without interrupting, then sharing one view calmly, which lowered Ajja's defensiveness.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak kept wanting to argue and got kicked under the table, but saw a calmer way of talking to Ajja.

grounding: Shows a young person asking a grandfather what shaped his views, listening without interrupting, then sharing one view calmly.
